---
title: "hyperparameter tuning"
---

## parameters vs hyperparameters

- parameters are learned from data during training — regression coefficients, a neural network's weights
- hyperparameters are set before training and control how learning happens — learning rate, tree depth, $k$ in knn, $\lambda$ in [regularisation](regularisation.qmd), number of folds, network architecture
- hyperparameters can't be chosen by minimising training loss directly — a sufficiently flexible model always reduces training error by overfitting, so they're chosen against a validation set or cross-validation instead, never the test set — see [train/test splits](train-test.qmd)

## search strategies

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| strategy | how it works | when to use |
|---|---|---|
| grid search | tries every combination on a predefined grid of values | few hyperparameters, small search space, want exhaustive coverage |
| random search | samples random combinations from specified ranges/distributions | more hyperparameters; often finds a good result faster than grid search for the same budget, since not every hyperparameter matters equally |
| bayesian optimisation | builds a probabilistic model of performance vs. hyperparameters, and picks the next candidate expected to improve most | expensive-to-train models where each trial counts; fewer trials needed than random search |

:::

- random search outperforms grid search in practice when only a few hyperparameters actually drive performance — grid search wastes trials varying unimportant ones at the same resolution as important ones
- bayesian optimisation and related methods (e.g. successive halving, hyperband) trade implementation complexity for sample efficiency when each candidate is costly to train

## evaluating each candidate

- score each candidate hyperparameter setting on a held-out validation set, or by averaging across folds in cross-validation
- use nested cross-validation when both tuning hyperparameters and getting an unbiased estimate of final performance matter — an inner loop tunes, an outer loop evaluates — see [train/test splits](train-test.qmd#cross-validation)
- once the best setting is chosen, refit on all available training data (train + validation) before the final test-set evaluation

## practical considerations

- the search space matters as much as the search strategy — log-scale ranges for learning rate or $\lambda$ (e.g. $10^{-4}$ to $10^{1}$) search more sensibly than linear ranges
- tuning many hyperparameters against a small validation set risks overfitting to that set itself; cross-validation or a larger validation set helps
- computational budget usually dictates the choice: grid/random search parallelise trivially across independent trials, while bayesian optimisation is sequential but needs far fewer trials
- preprocessing and feature engineering choices can also be tuned this way, not just model hyperparameters — but must be refit within each training fold to avoid leakage, see [feature engineering](feature-engineering.qmd#avoiding-leakage)
